question: What is considered a heavy period
answer: A heavy period (menorrhagia) is defined as bleeding that lasts more than 7 days, or soaking through one or more pads or tampons every hour for several consecutive hours, or passing blood clots larger than a quarter. Losing more than 80ml of blood per cycle is considered heavy. If your period interferes with daily activities, causes anemia, or requires double protection, it's likely too heavy and should be evaluated.

question: Why is my period so heavy
alternate_questions: Why do I bleed so much
answer: Heavy periods can be caused by: hormonal imbalances (especially progesterone deficiency), uterine fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, endometriosis, bleeding disorders (like von Willebrand disease), thyroid problems, PCOS, copper IUDs, certain medications, or perimenopause. Sometimes no cause is found. If your heavy bleeding is new or worsening, see a healthcare provider for evaluation, which may include blood tests, ultrasound, or biopsy.

question: Can fibroids cause heavy periods
alternate_questions: Why do fibroids cause heavy bleeding
answer: Yes, uterine fibroids are a very common cause of heavy periods. These benign muscle tumors in the uterus can increase the surface area of the uterine lining, distort blood vessels, and interfere with the uterus's ability to contract and stop bleeding. Submucosal fibroids (those bulging into the uterine cavity) are most likely to cause heavy bleeding. Fibroids may also cause pressure, frequent urination, and pelvic pain.

question: Can polyps cause heavy periods
answer: Yes, uterine polyps can cause heavy or irregular bleeding. These small, usually benign growths of endometrial tissue can develop in the uterus or cervix. They may cause heavy periods, bleeding between periods, or bleeding after sex. Polyps are more common in people in their 40s-50s and those who are overweight. They're usually diagnosed with ultrasound or hysteroscopy and can often be removed easily.

question: Can adenomyosis cause heavy periods
alternate_questions: Why does adenomyosis cause heavy flow
answer: Yes, adenomyosis commonly causes heavy, painful periods. In this condition, endometrial tissue grows into the muscular wall of the uterus, making the uterus enlarged, boggy, and prone to heavy bleeding. The displaced tissue bleeds during menstruation but has nowhere to exit, causing inflammation, pain, and heavy flow. Adenomyosis often coexists with endometriosis and is more common in people who have had children.

question: Can a copper IUD cause heavy periods
alternate_questions: Why is my period heavier with copper IUD
answer: Yes, copper IUDs commonly cause heavier, longer, and more painful periods, especially in the first 6-12 months after insertion. The copper creates a local inflammatory response in the uterus that increases prostaglandins, leading to more bleeding and cramping. For most people, this improves over time. If heavy bleeding is severe or doesn't improve after a year, talk to your provider about options. Hormonal IUDs often reduce bleeding instead.

question: Can bleeding disorders cause heavy periods
alternate_questions: Why do I bleed so much clotting
answer: Yes, bleeding disorders like von Willebrand disease can cause heavy periods. This is actually one of the most common symptoms in people with bleeding disorders. If you've had heavy periods since your very first period, bruise easily, have prolonged bleeding from cuts, or have family members with bleeding issues, ask your doctor about testing. A hematologist can do simple blood tests to check clotting function.

question: How do I manage heavy periods
answer: To manage heavy periods: Use high-absorbency products or double up (pad + tampon/cup). Change protection every 2-4 hours. Take iron supplements to prevent anemia. Use a heating pad for cramps. Stay hydrated. Track your flow. Try over-the-counter NSAIDs like ibuprofen, which can reduce bleeding. Wear dark clothing and keep spare supplies. For long-term management, talk to your doctor about hormonal treatments, tranexamic acid, or procedures.

question: What medications help heavy periods
answer: Medical treatments for heavy periods include: 1) Hormonal birth control (pill, patch, ring) to regulate cycles. 2) Hormonal IUD (Mirena, Kyleena) which often reduces bleeding by 90%. 3) Tranexamic acid (Lysteda) taken during periods to reduce bleeding. 4) NSAIDs like ibuprofen. 5) Progesterone-only treatments. 6) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists for short-term use. 7) Iron supplements for anemia. Discuss options with your healthcare provider.

question: Can heavy periods cause anemia
alternate_questions: Can I become anemic from my period
answer: Yes, heavy periods are a leading cause of iron-deficiency anemia in people who menstruate. Losing too much blood depletes iron stores faster than they can be replaced. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, shortness of breath, dizziness, and cravings for ice or non-food items (pica). A blood test can check your hemoglobin and ferritin levels. Treatment includes iron supplements and managing the heavy bleeding itself.

question: What foods help with heavy periods
alternate_questions: What to eat during heavy period
answer: For heavy periods, focus on iron-rich foods: red meat, dark leafy greens, lentils, beans, fortified cereals, and pumpkin seeds. Vitamin C helps iron absorption, so pair iron sources with citrus fruits, bell peppers, or tomatoes. Avoid excessive caffeine and dairy around iron-rich meals as they inhibit absorption. Anti-inflammatory foods like turmeric, ginger, and omega-3s may help. Stay hydrated and eat regular meals to maintain energy.

question: When should I see a doctor for heavy periods
alternate_questions: When is heavy period an emergency
answer: See a doctor if you: soak through a pad/tampon in an hour for 2+ hours, pass clots larger than a quarter, bleed for more than 7 days, have severe pain, feel faint or dizzy, show signs of anemia (extreme fatigue, shortness of breath), or if heavy bleeding is new or worsening. Seek emergency care for soaking through protection hourly with signs of shock (rapid heartbeat, confusion, extreme weakness).

question: Can endometriosis cause heavy periods
alternate_questions: Why does endometriosis cause heavy periods
answer: Yes, endometriosis can cause heavy periods, though it's more commonly associated with painful periods. Endometrial tissue growing outside the uterus responds to hormones and bleeds during menstruation, causing inflammation, pain, and sometimes heavier flow. Endometriosis may also cause bleeding between periods, pain during sex, and fertility issues. If you have heavy, painful periods with these additional symptoms, see a gynecologist.

question: Can hormonal imbalance cause heavy periods
alternate_questions: Why do hormones cause heavy flow
answer: Yes, hormonal imbalances are a very common cause of heavy periods. Specifically, insufficient progesterone relative to estrogen (sometimes called estrogen dominance) can cause the uterine lining to build up excessively and then shed heavily. This often occurs with anovulatory cycles, PCOS, perimenopause, and thyroid disorders. Hormonal treatments like birth control or progesterone therapy can help regulate this balance.

question: What is tranexamic acid for periods
answer: Tranexamic acid (brand name Lysteda) is a prescription medication that reduces heavy menstrual bleeding by helping blood clot. You take it only during your period, usually for up to 5 days. It can reduce bleeding by 30-50% without hormonal side effects. It's not suitable for people with a history of blood clots. Side effects are usually mild (headache, nausea). It's a good option for those who want to avoid hormones.

question: Can I use a menstrual cup with heavy periods
answer: Yes, menstrual cups are excellent for heavy periods! High-capacity cups (30-40ml) can hold more than a super tampon and can be worn for up to 12 hours. Cups measure your flow, which helps track heavy bleeding. They're also cost-effective and eco-friendly. For very heavy days, you might need to empty more frequently. Some people use a backup pad for extra security. Make sure to choose a cup with adequate capacity and firmness.

question: Can exercise help heavy periods
answer: Moderate exercise may help regulate hormones and reduce heavy bleeding over time, but intense exercise during heavy flow days can sometimes worsen symptoms. Gentle activities like walking, yoga, and swimming are beneficial. Some studies suggest regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity and hormonal balance, which can help with cycle-related issues. However, exercise alone is unlikely to resolve significantly heavy periods caused by fibroids or other structural issues.

question: Can stress cause heavy periods
alternate_questions: Why does stress make periods heavier
answer: While stress more commonly delays or lightens periods, chronic stress can sometimes contribute to heavy or irregular bleeding by disrupting hormonal balance. Stress affects the hypothalamus-pituitary-ovary axis, potentially causing anovulatory cycles that lead to heavy breakthrough bleeding. Managing stress through meditation, therapy, exercise, and adequate sleep supports overall hormonal health and may help regulate flow.

question: What surgical options exist for heavy periods
answer: Surgical options for heavy periods include: 1) Endometrial ablation: destroys the uterine lining, reduces bleeding significantly, but not for those wanting future pregnancy. 2) Myomectomy: removes fibroids while preserving the uterus. 3) Uterine artery embolization: blocks blood flow to fibroids. 4) Hysterectomy: removal of the uterus, definitive but major surgery. These are considered after less invasive treatments fail. Discuss risks, benefits, and fertility desires with your surgeon.

question: Can birth control pills help heavy periods
answer: Yes, combined birth control pills are very effective for heavy periods. They regulate hormones, reduce the uterine lining buildup, and can decrease bleeding by up to 60%. Many people find their periods become lighter, shorter, and more predictable. The pill can also help with cramps and PMS. If you're not trying to conceive, this is often a first-line treatment. Your doctor can help find the right formulation for you.
